_note: Shared treasure data for monster_gen.py and idea_gen.py, loaded through
scripts/_treasure.py. Two datasets live here because they answer two halves of
the same question: 'how much is it worth' and 'what does it look like'.
value_table
The core rulebook's 1-18 finding-treasure table (Monsters chapter, 'Treasure'),
transcribed to match the book. DO NOT reword these entries - they are canon,
and an earlier hand-edited second copy in idea_gen.py silently drifted at
entries 12 and 13, which is why this file exists. Each entry is:
template  a format string; every {placeholder} must appear in dice, except
{weight}, which is derived as max(1, coins // 100).
dice      placeholder -> dice expression, NdS or NdS*M. Rolled by the
caller so a GM never receives '2d8 or so' and has to roll again.
object    present and true when the entry IS a physical object whose
appearance is left abstract ('a small valuable item worth 140
coins' says what it is worth, not what it is). Only those entries
get appearance options composed from the 'objects' tables below.
Be strict about this flag - it is the whole test for whether a
GM is offered a menu of looks. Coins (1, 3, 7, 11) and knowledge
(6, 15, 16, 17) are not objects and offering 'a pewter idol'
beside 'many bags of coins' is noise. Entry 2 ('an item useful to
the current situation') and entry 10 ('a magical item or effect')
are left unflagged for a different reason: the objects tables
below are art and valuables, which do not describe a useful tool,
and an 'effect' may not be a thing at all. For magic items reach
for references/magic-items.md or idea_gen.py std-magicitem.
The two scripts roll INTO this table differently and that is intentional.
monster_gen.py rolls the monster's damage die plus tag bonuses; idea_gen.py
has no monster and therefore no damage die, so it rolls an exploding d6.
Share the data, not the roll.
roll_again
Entries that give their own result AND send the roller back for another.
objects
Composable appearance tables. Each is independently rollable so a GM can ask
for just a material without rerolling a whole object, and the composer draws
across them to offer whole objects. These are PROMPTING MATERIAL - a rolled
object is a suggestion to describe from, not a line to read aloud.
object_type entries carry traits, and the traits are what keep a composed
object coherent rather than mad-libs. Without them 'a marble potion engraved
with a portrait' is a legal roll. The composer understands:
gem           the object IS a stone: named from color + gem_type, no
material (the stone is its own material)
gem_optional  may be set with a stone, one time in three
depicts       can carry a motif - something is shown or engraved on it
liquid        has no material of its own; the material describes its vessel
An object_type with no traits is just material + name + condition + provenance.
WHEN ADDING AN object_type, SET ITS TRAITS DELIBERATELY. The failure mode is
silent: a missing 'depicts' only means that object never gets a motif, which
reads as blandness rather than as a bug. tools/validate_skill.py checks that
every trait the composer knows about is used by at least one entry, and that
no category is empty, but it cannot tell you a trait is missing from an entry
that wanted one.
material, color and gem_type entries are used ATTRIBUTIVELY - they land in
front of a noun ('a {material} {object}', 'a {color} {gem_type}'). So each one
must read as an adjective phrase, not a clause: 'nameless dull metal' works,
'a metal nobody present can name' produces 'an a metal nobody present can name
amulet'. Put clause-shaped flavour in condition or provenance instead, which
are appended after a comma and can be full phrases.
material is tiered: 'mundane' is the default and 'exotic' comes up one time in
six, so an exotic material stays a genuine event rather than the house style.
Keep exotic entries strange but placeable - a GM should be able to build a
question out of one ('who works starmetal, and where did this come from?').
